newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France seeks to allay budget deficit fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France seeks to allay budget deficit fears.

text.p: France's new Socialist-government, seeking to allay fears over public finances, insisted on Thursday it would act to curb the public deficit and said a pick-up in growth would work in its favour.
"There is no reason for markets to be worried," Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told reporters after a weekly cabinet meeting.

Earlier financial daily La Tribune said an audit of public finances due on July 21 was likely to show a deficit this year of 3.6 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product -- well above the 3.0 targeted by the previous government.

Afternoon daily Le Monde also published extracts from a letter by former prime minister Alain Juppe warning the new government that the deficit could worsen to above four percent next year without tough action.
Strauss-Kahn repeated that he was awaiting the results of the audit before taking any action needed and said economic growth was improving.
"Growth is returning in a stronger way than we thought a few weeks ago," he said.
Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said Paris aimed to cut the public deficit without imposing austerity.
She said France wanted to reach a position close to that of Germany and said it was not clear whether even Bonn could reduce its public deficit to exactly 3.0 percent of GDP as planned.
"What has been held out by Germany for now is the respect of the 3.0 percent target. Will they make it? There is debate even in Germany on that point," she told a news conference.
"It is clear that, for France, its wish is, of course, to be able to have positions that meet those of its neighbouring country," she said.
Economists expect that the French government will try to reduce the deficit this year to around 3.3 percent of GDP, in line with the level that many expect for Germany.
The 3.6 to 3.7 percent GDP/deficit ratio cited in La Tribune was roughly in line with market expectations. Strauss-Kahn has said the figure could be between 3.4 and 3.8 percent.

UBS economist Eric Muller said the figures, if confirmed, would allay the worst fears that the deficit would be 3.8 percent or more, a level that might have tempted the new government to seek a delay to monetary union.
"It allows them to say, we are going to correct it. We will correct what we find," he said.
But it was also clear that the government would not be able to cut the deficit to 3.0 percent. Strauss-Kahn has already said France would not make 3.0 percent this year.
But while the government may be able to finesse its deficit overshoot this year, it faces a tough task in 1998 in reducing it further to three percent.
Crucially, it will lack a special one-off transfer of funds from France Telecom -- worth 37.5 billion francs ($6.3 billion) or 0.45 percent of GDP -- which helped reduce the deficit this year.

Juppe, in a letter dated June 2, the day after Socialist-led parliamentary election victory, spelled out the likely path in words unpalatable for a government which promised to end austerity and boost growth and jobs.

"The initial work on the budget outlook carried out by the budget ministry experts suggests a trend in public deficits to a figure above four percent of GDP, based, it is true, on particularly low forecasts for revenues," Le Monde quoted Juppe's letter as saying.
"This figure could be reduced to three percent after savings on budget and welfare spending, questioning some fiscal spending and tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues," it said.

Economists say the government is likely to try to cut the deficit next year by scrapping income tax cuts promised by the previous government and seeking new one-off transfers similar to the France Telecom funds while also capping public spending. ($ = 5.959 French Francs)
